clinical.body: Pivoting or an awkward landing can produce a pop, swelling and giving way. Clinical assessment also considers menisci, cartilage and other ligaments; symptoms alone do not identify an isolated ACL injury.

pathology.body: Injury ranges from stretching to partial or complete disruption. An attachment injury can pull off a bone fragment. Associated damage matters as well as the ACL tear itself.

mri.body: MRI assesses the ACL and associated meniscal, cartilage and ligament injuries. It supports clinical assessment; it is not always necessary to establish the diagnosis.

xray.body: Radiographs assess accompanying bone injury, including avulsion. They do not directly demonstrate an ACL tear.

selfCheck.question: Does a normal radiograph establish that the ACL is intact?
selfCheck.answer: No. Radiographs show bone rather than directly establishing ligament continuity.

lesson.anatomy: Cruciate ligament connecting posterior tibial intercondylar region to medial femoral condyle.
lesson.function: Restrains posterior tibial translation relative to femur.

extended.modelLimit: The model has one PCL selection, not separate functional bundles or a simulated posterior-drawer examination. Source shape cannot establish ligament competence.

clinical.body: A force against the front of a flexed knee, such as a dashboard impact, can injure the PCL. Assessment includes posterior laxity and possible accompanying injuries.

pathology.body: Partial tears and combined knee injuries occur. A tibial attachment may avulse with bone; ligament appearance alone does not establish functional stability.

mri.body: MRI depicts the PCL better than radiographs. Chronic injury may look deceptively normal, so imaging must be interpreted with history and examination.

xray.body: Look for an associated bony avulsion. Clinician-directed stress radiographs can assess posterior translation; the atlas does not reproduce this examination.

selfCheck.question: Why can apparently normal chronic imaging be insufficient?
selfCheck.answer: PCL injury may be less conspicuous later; clinical posterior laxity still needs assessment.

lesson.anatomy: Medial knee ligament between femur and tibia.
lesson.function: Helps resist valgus opening.

extended.modelLimit: Superficial/deep MCL and meniscal attachments are not individually labelled here. Do not equate one displayed surface with the complete medial stabilizing complex.

clinical.body: Valgus loading may cause medial pain, tenderness and instability. Examine for other knee injuries rather than assuming an isolated sprain.

pathology.body: A sprain can stretch, partly disrupt or completely tear the ligament; attachment avulsion is possible.

mri.body: MRI evaluates the ligament injury and other knee structures; grading also depends on clinical assessment.

xray.body: Radiographs may show attachment avulsion, not the ligament tear itself.

ultrasound.body: Follow the MCL along the medial joint line to its tibial attachment. Ultrasound can assess accessible fibres dynamically; this surface does not reproduce the layered examination.

selfCheck.question: Which side of the knee is assessed for an MCL injury?
selfCheck.answer: The medial side; pain and instability still require assessment of accompanying injuries.

lesson.anatomy: Lateral knee ligament between femur and fibular head.

extended.modelLimit: This fibular collateral ligament is not the entire posterolateral corner. Additional stabilizers and nerve relationships are incomplete in this specimen.

clinical.body: Varus loading can injure the lateral ligament, producing lateral tenderness or instability. Associated injuries affect the overall assessment.

pathology.body: Partial or complete disruption and bony attachment avulsion can occur. A visible ligament is not proof of mechanical competence.

mri.body: MRI assesses the LCL together with other ligaments, cartilage and menisci.

xray.body: Radiographs may reveal an avulsed fragment but do not directly show an LCL tear.

ultrasound.body: The fibular head helps identify the LCL course. Distinguish it from biceps femoris posteriorly and the deeper proximal popliteus tendon; the anatomy is not interchangeable.

selfCheck.question: Does an LCL view show all lateral stabilizers?
selfCheck.answer: No. It is one ligament; the specimen does not supply a complete posterolateral-corner study.

lesson.anatomy: Connects patella to tibial tuberosity.
lesson.function: Transmits extensor force to the tibia.

extended.modelLimit: The source label is patellar ligament; clinical literature often calls it patellar tendon. No separate enthesis, tendon lamina or tear is mapped.

clinical.body: A traumatic pop, infrapatellar gap and impaired active knee extension suggest extensor-mechanism injury. Clinical examination distinguishes this from other causes of pain or weakness.

pathology.body: Partial or complete disruption may occur, including avulsion at the patella. Tendinopathy and tendon rupture are different findings; neither is demonstrated by this source surface.

mri.body: MRI can show the site and amount of disrupted tendon, and help distinguish other injuries with similar symptoms.

xray.body: A high-positioned patella can accompany loss of distal tethering. Radiographic patellar height is not measured by this atlas.

ultrasound.body: Trace the tendon between patella and tibia in long and short axes. Include the tendon width: abnormalities need not lie in the midline.

selfCheck.question: Why may the patella move upward after complete distal tendon disruption?
selfCheck.answer: The connection to the tibia is lost while the quadriceps can pull proximally.

lesson.anatomy: Grouped source menisci; medial and lateral parts are not separately selectable.
lesson.function: Menisci distribute knee loads and improve joint congruity.

extended.modelLimit: Medial and lateral menisci remain one source group. Horns, roots, tear zones and displaced fragments are not separate selections; a displayed gap must not be labelled as a tear.

clinical.body: Joint-line pain, swelling and catching or locking can accompany a meniscal injury, but are not specific. Acute tears may coexist with ACL injury.

pathology.body: Traumatic and degenerative tears differ in context. Radial, flap and displaced bucket-handle patterns are examples, not interchangeable labels for every symptomatic meniscus.

mri.body: MRI is commonly used to evaluate acute meniscal tears and associated soft-tissue injury. Location and pattern require review of the real image series.

xray.body: A meniscal tear is not directly visible on radiographs; bone and degenerative joint changes may offer alternative explanations for pain.

ct.body: CT arthrography may be considered when MRI cannot be obtained. It uses joint contrast and is not equivalent to routine non-contrast CT.

selfCheck.question: Can this grouped mesh locate a medial meniscal root tear?
selfCheck.answer: No. It has no separately validated roots or tear mapping; patient imaging would need independent interpretation.

lesson.anatomy: Shared quadriceps attachment to the patella.
lesson.function: Conveys quadriceps force into the extensor apparatus.

extended.modelLimit: One tendon surface is supplied. Laminar contributions, retinacula and tear gaps are not segmented; moving the tendon away is not a rupture simulation.

clinical.body: Pain and a gap above the patella with loss of active extension raise concern for extensor-mechanism disruption. A new traumatic loss of extension needs clinical assessment.

pathology.body: Tears may be partial, complete or detach from the patella. Existing tendon weakness can contribute; a complete tear interrupts force transmission to the patella.

mri.body: MRI can define tear location and extent when needed, including partial versus complete disruption or an alternative injury.

xray.body: A low-positioned patella on a lateral radiograph can accompany quadriceps tendon rupture. Interpret position with the examination, not from this mesh.

ultrasound.body: Inspect the tendon above the patella in longitudinal and transverse planes. Probe-angle effects can alter its appearance; the model has neither echotexture nor a simulated ultrasound beam.

selfCheck.question: Which patellar displacement may accompany a quadriceps tendon rupture?
selfCheck.answer: Inferior displacement: the intact patellar tendon can pull the patella downward.

clinical.body: Axial loading after a fall may injure the heel and other sites, including the spine. Examination includes skin, circulation, sensation and associated trauma.

pathology.body: Fracture can widen or shorten the heel and disrupt the subtalar joint. Articular injury may lead to persistent pain, stiffness and post-traumatic arthritis.

xray.body: Radiographs demonstrate calcaneal fracture and displacement. Clinical findings and appropriate additional views remain important.

ct.body: CT helps define fragment displacement and joint involvement in this complex bone, complementing radiographs rather than replacing clinical assessment.

selfCheck.question: Which nearby joint often matters in a calcaneal fracture?
selfCheck.answer: The subtalar joint: articular disruption can contribute to later pain and restricted movement.

clinical.body: Severe ankle pain after high-energy trauma requires assessment of bone alignment, skin, circulation, sensation and associated injuries. A talar injury is not simply an ankle sprain.

pathology.body: Fractures can involve the neck, body or processes. Displacement may compromise blood supply, with later osteonecrosis or post-traumatic arthritis; risk is not established from this model.

xray.body: Radiographs show fracture and alignment. Persistent clinical concern may require further imaging even if the initial view is inconclusive.

ct.body: CT resolves fracture lines and displacement in cross-section, helping characterize complex talar injury. Rotating this surface is not a CT reconstruction of a fracture.

selfCheck.question: Why does blood supply matter in a displaced talar fracture?
selfCheck.answer: Vascular disruption can lead to osteonecrosis and collapse despite fracture treatment.

clinical.body: Sudden posterior ankle pain or a pop with reduced push-off raises concern for rupture. Clinicians assess tendon continuity and the calf-squeeze response alongside the history.

pathology.body: Rupture may be partial or complete and occur within the tendon or at its calcaneal attachment. Tendon degeneration and traumatic disruption are not synonymous.

mri.body: MRI can assess tear extent and location and identify alternative soft-tissue causes of symptoms.

xray.body: Insertional avulsion may leave a small calcaneal fragment visible on radiographs. Absence of a fragment does not establish tendon continuity.

ultrasound.body: Ultrasound can show tendon continuity and changes with ankle movement in real time. This atlas is static source geometry, not a dynamic scan or tendon-gap measurement.

selfCheck.question: Does a normal bone radiograph exclude Achilles rupture?
selfCheck.answer: No. A tendon can rupture without an avulsed bone fragment.
